chunks.title: Snow Day Calculator — Will School Close Tomorrow?
chunks.text:
Enter your ZIP code above — the calculator pulls the live 24-hour forecast for your area (expected snowfall, overnight low, wind, and 4–7 AM conditions) and turns it into a transparent probability score. Scores above 75% mean a snow day is very likely; below 20% means unlikely.
There is no fixed number — it varies by district, road conditions, and timing. As a rough rule, many US districts start considering closures around 4–6 inches (10–15 cm) of overnight snow, but extreme cold (below about −15°C / 5°F) or high winds can close schools with much less snow. Our scoring model reflects this: snowfall sets the base score, cold and wind add to it.
It is an estimate based on live forecast data, not a guarantee — school districts weigh road crews, bus safety, and building conditions too. Forecasts are most reliable 12–24 hours out, so check again the evening before and early morning. Read our full accuracy breakdown for the honest details.

chunks.title: Snow Day Predictor — How Snow Day Prediction Works | SnowDayPlanner
chunks.text:
Prediction is part meteorology, part local knowledge. Here is how it really works — then try it live for your ZIP code.
Free, no account needed. We use live weather data for your area.
# The two halves of a prediction
Half one is the atmosphere: how much snow will fall, when, at what temperature, with what wind. Modern hourly forecast models are quite good at this 12–36 hours out — which is exactly the window that matters for school decisions.
Half two is the ground: plowed roads, bus routes on hills, wind chill at the bus stop, whether the storm hits at 2 AM or 2 PM. No weather model knows your district's road crews. A good predictor is honest about this split — ours shows you the weather half as a transparent score and tells you plainly that the district decides the rest.
# The district decision timeline
Evening before (8–10 PM): superintendents watch the overnight forecast; some districts announce early for big storms.
4–5 AM: the classic decision window — officials drive the roads and check actual accumulation.
5–6 AM: announcements go out via district alerts, local news, and robocalls.

chunks.title: Snow Day Predictor — How Snow Day Prediction Works | SnowDayPlanner
chunks.text:
This timeline is why timing matters so much in our model: snow falling between 4–7 AM local time gets a +10% adjustment, because it lands exactly when buses roll.
# Predictor vs. calculator — what's the difference?
Honestly? On this site they share the same engine. The Snow Day Calculator is the quick tool — enter a ZIP, get a score. This predictor page is the explanation — why the score means what it means, and how districts turn forecasts into decisions. Same math, deeper context. Our formula page documents every step.

chunks.title: Is It a Snow Day Today? Morning Checklist | SnowDayPlanner
chunks.text:
# Is It a Snow Day Today?
Woke up to snow? Get the current picture — then verify it the way districts actually announce.
Free, no account needed. We use live weather data for your area.
# Morning-of checklist (do this first)
Check your district's website or alert feed — this is the only official source.
Check local TV news school-closing tickers (they update from 5 AM).
Look outside at YOUR street, not just the forecast — side roads decide bus routes.
If in doubt, keep kids home-safe: an unexcused absence beats an unsafe commute.
# What the score means this morning
Run fresh — the tool always uses the latest hourly data. A high score this morning with snow still falling means conditions are actively bad; a high score with snow already stopped may mean plows have caught up. Timing beats totals on the morning of the storm.
# Delays vs. full closures
Many districts use 2-hour delays instead of full snow days when roads need just a bit more time. A delay announcement can also upgrade to a closure — keep checking until the buses actually run.
# Worked example: the 6 AM decision

chunks.title: Is It a Snow Day Today? Morning Checklist | SnowDayPlanner
chunks.text:
Say you wake at 5:30 AM to 5 inches of new snow, with the back edge of the storm still two hours away, and your score reads 86%. What happens next matters more than the number. Plows have been working the main routes since 3 AM, but your subdivision has not seen a truck yet — and buses cannot safely run unplowed side streets. In this setup, most districts announce a 2-hour delay by about 6:00 AM, then re-drive the routes around 8:00 AM. If the snow has not eased by then, the delay converts to a full closure. So set two check-ins — one now, one at 8:00 AM — and do not send kids to the bus stop on the strength of the first announcement alone.
# Common questions on the morning of
Can a delay still become a closure? Yes. Districts re-check the worst routes mid-morning, and a 2-hour delay announced at 6 AM can convert to a full closure by 8 AM if conditions worsen or plows fall behind.
My street is clear — why is school still closed? Buses serve the whole district, including its steepest hill and its last-plowed neighborhood. The call is based on the hardest route the buses must run, not the average street.

chunks.title: Is It a Snow Day Today? Morning Checklist | SnowDayPlanner
chunks.text: Can I trust this morning's score? The score is computed from live hourly data, not last night's forecast — so re-run it this morning instead of relying on a screenshot or a score you saw yesterday evening.

chunks.title: Will There Be a Snow Day Tomorrow? | SnowDayPlanner
chunks.text:
# Will There Be a Snow Day Tomorrow?
The overnight forecast decides most snow days. Get your live score now — then know when to check back.
Free, no account needed. We use live weather data for your area.
# When will you actually know?
Big, obvious storms: many districts announce the evening before, often 8–10 PM.
Borderline storms: the 4–6 AM window — officials check real road conditions at dawn.
Announcements come via district text alerts, websites, local TV, and robocalls — sign up for your district's alert system now, before you need it.
# What matters most for “tomorrow”
Overnight accumulation is king. Snow that falls between midnight and 6 AM — before plows finish and buses roll — drives most closure decisions. That is why our model gives a +10% adjustment to snow in the 4–7 AM window: it is the highest-signal period in the whole forecast.
# Your evening checklist
Run the calculator now for tonight's forecast snapshot.
Check again after 9 PM — evening model runs sharpen the overnight picture.
Set an alarm 30 minutes early and re-check district announcements at 5:30 AM.
Have a backup childcare plan whenever the score is above 40%.
# Worked example: a 55% evening

chunks.title: Will There Be a Snow Day Tomorrow? | SnowDayPlanner
chunks.text:
At 8 PM, the forecast shows 4 inches arriving between 1 AM and 7 AM, with the heaviest band landing right in the 4–7 AM window — your score sits at 55%, the genuinely uncertain zone. Here is how to read it: if the storm tracks 20 miles north, your district catches the edge and a delay is the likely call. If it tracks south and the 4–7 AM burst verifies, totals reach 6 inches before buses roll and most districts close. Neither outcome is knowable at 8 PM. The honest move is to prepare for both: childcare on standby, the alarm set early, and a final check at 5:30 AM — when the overnight snow is measured fact, not forecast.
# Prep tonight for either outcome
An uncertain score is not a wasted evening — it is the signal to get the cheap, reversible preparation done now:
Confirm the backup childcare arrangement and make sure that person knows they might be needed.
Charge laptops and tablets, and find the remote-learning login details before you need them at 7 AM.
Lay out boots, coats, hats, and gloves tonight — hunting for them at dawn wastes the margin you saved.
Move the car to the end of the driveway so a plow berm does not trap you in the morning.

chunks.title: Will There Be a Snow Day Tomorrow? | SnowDayPlanner
chunks.text: Set two alarms: one for the 5:30 AM announcement check, one as the normal wake-up in case school runs.

chunks.title: School Closing Predictor — How Districts Decide | SnowDayPlanner
chunks.text:
# School Closing Predictor
Snow forecasts start the conversation — but districts decide on much more. Here is the full picture.
Free, no account needed. We use live weather data for your area.
# The factors districts actually weigh
Road conditions on bus routes — especially hills, rural roads, and neighborhoods plowed last.
Timing: overnight snow before 6 AM is far more disruptive than afternoon snow.
Temperature and wind chill at bus-stop time — extreme cold closes schools with no snow at all.
Building readiness: heat, parking lots, sidewalks, and whether staff can get in.
Forecast confidence: a certain 8 inches closes schools; a possible 3 inches often doesn't.
# Why neighboring districts disagree
One district closes while the next stays open — and both can be right. Plow fleets, geography, and policy differ street by street. Urban districts with big fleets rarely close; rural districts with long bus routes close more easily. Your district's history is the best predictor of its future calls.
# What our score covers (and what it can't)

chunks.title: School Closing Predictor — How Districts Decide | SnowDayPlanner
chunks.text:
The calculator scores the weather half — snowfall, cold, wind, timing — from live forecast data, with the formula published openly . It cannot know your district's plows, policies, or past habits. Use the score as the weather input to your own judgment, then confirm with official district channels.
# Inside the 5 AM decision
Here is how the call actually happens in most districts. Around 3:30–4:00 AM, the transportation director — or a designated driver — physically drives the district's hilliest, most rural bus routes: the forecast is background; the windshield is the evidence. By 4:30 AM they are on a call with neighboring superintendents and the county road commission, comparing what each district is seeing on the ground. The hard deadline is about 5:00 AM, because the first buses roll soon after and drivers need to know whether to come in. That is why announcements cluster between 5:30 and 6:00 AM — and why a district that is still "waiting to see" after 5 AM usually ends up staying open: the buses are already out.
# Reading your score like a decision-maker
Under 20%: plan a normal morning. Closures at this level are rare, and usually driven by extreme cold rather than snow.

chunks.title: School Closing Predictor — How Districts Decide | SnowDayPlanner
chunks.text:
20–50%: the gray zone. Check official announcements before waking the kids, and keep a loose backup plan in mind.
50–80%: arrange real backup childcare tonight. Facing these odds, most districts delay or close.
Above 80%: expect a closure or a delay — but still confirm on official district channels before changing work plans. The district's call, not the score, is final.

chunks.title: Ice Day Calculator — Will School Close for Ice? (Free) | SnowDayPlanner
chunks.text:
Snow gets the headlines — but ice closes schools faster. Check your ice risk now.
Free, no account needed. We use live weather data for your area.
# Why ice days happen with almost no snow
An ice day is a school closure caused by freezing rain or refrozen melt — not snowfall. A thin glaze of ice makes roads and sidewalks impassable for buses even when the snowfall total is near zero. Districts treat ice as more dangerous than snow because plows cannot clear it and salt works slowly below −10°C.
# How we score ice risk
Every result on this site includes an ice risk rating — Low, Moderate, or High. We flag ice risk when the forecast shows precipitation falling while temperatures hover near 0°C, the classic freezing-rain setup. The longer that window lasts, the higher the risk. Ice risk feeds into your travel and driving-risk scores too.
# Ice day safety checklist
Assume every wet surface is icy when temperatures are near freezing — especially bridges and shaded sidewalks.
Give buses and plows extra room; stopping distances on ice can triple.
Charge devices and know your district's announcement channel — ice decisions often come earlier than snow calls.

chunks.title: Ice Day Calculator — Will School Close for Ice? (Free) | SnowDayPlanner
chunks.text:
If school runs on an ice-risk morning, leave 15 minutes early and stick to treated main roads.
# Ice vs. snow: which closes school more often?
Per inch of precipitation, ice wins. Two centimeters of snow rarely closes anything; a few millimeters of freezing rain can shut down a whole district. That is why our calculator scores ice risk separately — a 10% snow day score with High ice risk still deserves your attention. See how the full formula works .

chunks.title: School Delay Calculator — 2-Hour Delay Predictor (Free) | SnowDayPlanner
chunks.text:
# School Delay Calculator
Not every storm closes school — many just delay it. Check your delay risk now.
Free, no account needed. We use live weather data for your area.
# Delay vs. closure: how districts decide
A 2-hour delay is the middle ground districts choose when conditions are bad at 6 AM but expected to improve — for example, when plows need one more pass, or temperatures rise above freezing by 9 AM. Delays are far more common than full closures: many districts issue several delays for every closure.
# How we score delay risk
Every result includes a separate delay risk score. It runs lower than closure risk by design: light snow (2–5 cm), marginal temperatures, and morning-only hazards push delay risk up without pushing closure risk. If delay risk is high while closure risk is low, expect a late start rather than a day off.
# What a 2-hour delay means for your morning
Buses run 2 hours late — the pickup time shifts, the route doesn't.
Morning kindergarten and early programs are often cancelled.
Breakfast may not be served — plan accordingly.
After-school activities usually run as normal unless the district says otherwise.

chunks.title: School Delay Calculator — 2-Hour Delay Predictor (Free) | SnowDayPlanner
chunks.text:
Delays can become closures: if conditions don't improve, districts upgrade the call by ~7 AM.
# When delays turn into closures
Watch the storm risk and travel risk scores alongside delay risk. When all three climb together, the district is likely weighing a full closure. Our school closing predictor explains the full decision picture.

chunks.title: Michigan Snow Day Calculator — Free MI School Closing Predictor | SnowDayPlanner
chunks.text:
# Michigan Snow Day Calculator
Lake-effect snow makes Michigan a snow day capital. Check your chances now.
Free, no account needed. We use live weather data for your area.
# Why Michigan gets so many snow days
Michigan sits between three Great Lakes, and lake-effect snow can dump a foot of snow on one county while the next stays dry. West Michigan (Grand Rapids, Muskegon) and the Upper Peninsula are the hardest hit. Fast-moving Alberta clippers add frequent light snowfalls that stack up through the week.
# How Michigan districts decide
Most Michigan districts watch the 4–7 AM window — our calculator weights it too.
Rural districts with long bus routes close more easily; try the rural school type above.
Wind off the lakes causes blowing snow and whiteouts even after plowing — wind is a major factor here.
Extreme cold days (below −10°C wind chill) close Michigan schools with no snow at all.
# Michigan snow day tips

chunks.title: Michigan Snow Day Calculator — Free MI School Closing Predictor | SnowDayPlanner
chunks.text: Lake-effect bands are narrow and intense — a 20-mile difference can flip your score. If you live near Lake Michigan, check both your home ZIP and your school's ZIP when they differ. Districts typically announce by 5:30–6:00 AM; have a backup plan ready the night before when our storm risk score is high. For the full methodology, see how the calculator works .

chunks.title: How the Snow Day Calculator Works (Full Formula) | SnowDayPlanner
chunks.text:
# How the Snow Day Calculator Works
No black box. Here is the exact formula behind every score — so you can judge it for yourself.
# The formula in 30 seconds
Expected snowfall in the next 24 hours sets a base score . Then three adjustments are added for extreme cold, high wind, and snow during the 4–7 AM commute window. The result is capped at 95% — a forecast is never certain.
# Step 1 — base score from snowfall
We take the maximum expected snowfall (cm) in the next 24 hours:
Values between these points are interpolated (e.g. 7.5 cm ≈ 62%).
Overnight low below −10°C: +5% (extreme cold alone can close schools)
Wind over 40 km/h: +10% (blowing snow, wind chill, drifting)
Snow falling between 4–7 AM local time: +10% (hits buses and the morning commute)
School type: urban/rural public +10%, private −10%, college −15% (different schools close at different thresholds)
# Step 2b — beyond the score: risks, ice & confidence
The single percentage is not the whole story. Every result also shows:
Risk breakdown — separate closure, delay, travel, storm, and driving-risk scores, so you can see which danger is driving the number.

chunks.title: How the Snow Day Calculator Works (Full Formula) | SnowDayPlanner
chunks.text:
Ice risk — freezing rain creates dangerous ice even with little snow; we flag Low, Moderate, or High ice risk from precipitation falling near 0°C.
Confidence — High when the forecast is strong and consistent, lower when models disagree or the score sits in the uncertain middle.
Recommendation — a plain-language read on what the numbers mean for your morning.
# Step 3 — verdict bands
75% and above — Very likely
# Where the data comes from
Your ZIP or postal code is converted to coordinates with a free geocoding service — or use the location button to check via GPS — then we fetch hourly forecast data (temperature, snowfall, wind speed, humidity, visibility) from Open-Meteo, a free weather API. Results are cached for one hour, because forecasts update hourly.
# What the score deliberately ignores
Honesty matters more than a bigger number. The score does not know your district's plowing capacity, bus fleet, or past closure habits — and those decide real closures. That is why every result is labelled an estimate, and why you should always confirm with your district.

chunks.title: How Accurate Is the Snow Day Calculator? (Honest Answer) | SnowDayPlanner
chunks.text:
# How Accurate Is the Snow Day Calculator?
The honest answer: it is a good estimate of the weather side of the decision — not a crystal ball for what your district will do.
# What the score is actually predicting
The calculator predicts weather conditions that typically lead to closures — heavy snow, extreme cold, dangerous wind. It does not predict your superintendent's decision. Districts also weigh road-crew readiness, bus safety, building heat, and even the day of the week.
# Where it is strongest
Clear-cut storms: 15+ cm overnight with high wind → scores 85–95%, and closures are genuinely very likely.
Clear non-events: no snow and mild temps → scores under 10%, and school almost always runs normally.
Timing: snow arriving 4–7 AM is the highest-signal window — the model weights it explicitly.
Borderline storms (3–6 cm): the hardest calls in real life too — districts split roughly half the time. Expect scores of 40–60% here, which correctly means “coin flip.”
Fast-changing forecasts: a storm track shifting 50 miles overnight can flip the outcome. Forecasts are most reliable 12–24 hours out.

chunks.title: How Accurate Is the Snow Day Calculator? (Honest Answer) | SnowDayPlanner
chunks.text:
Extreme-cold closures: thresholds vary hugely by region (−25°C closes schools in Minnesota; −10°C can do it in Texas).
District quirks: some districts almost never close; others close early. The model cannot know local policy.
Check the evening before AND early morning — forecasts sharpen overnight.
Treat 40–65% as “prepare for either outcome,” not as a prediction of closure.
Always confirm with your district's official announcements, hotline, or local news.
We publish the full formula so anyone can audit it, and we will never inflate scores to look “bolder.” A calculator that admits uncertainty is more useful than one that pretends at certainty.

chunks.title: About SnowDayPlanner | SnowDayPlanner
chunks.text:
A free tool that answers one winter question honestly: what are the chances of a snow day?
SnowDayPlanner is a free snow day probability calculator. Enter a US ZIP code or Canadian postal code and get a live score (0–95%) built from the next 24 hours of forecast data — snowfall, temperature, wind, and timing.
Most prediction tools are black boxes. We publish our full scoring formula so you can see exactly where every point comes from — and judge for yourself whether to trust it. We would rather show uncertainty honestly than fake certainty.
We are not a weather service and not affiliated with any school district. Our scores are estimates from forecast data; districts make the final closure decisions based on road conditions, buses, and local policy. Always confirm with official district announcements.
Geocoding via api.zippopotam.us; weather data via Open-Meteo. Both are free public services — which is why this tool is free, with no account needed.

chunks.title: Alaska Winter Storm Oct 19–22, 2026: Closures & Safety | SnowDayPlanner
chunks.text:
# Alaska Winter Storm Oct 19–22, 2026: Closures & Safety
Interior Alaska is in the path of a major early-season winter storm, and the takeaway for families is simple: expect heavy snow, dangerous travel, and likely school closures this week. The National Weather Service (NWS) office in Fairbanks has Winter Storm Warnings in effect across much of the Interior through Thursday, October 22 . Forecasters expect 12 to 30 inches of snow, up to 36 inches in the Eastern Alaska Range above 2,500 feet, and wind gusts of 60 to 65 mph . The NWS warns travel will become “very difficult to impossible.”
Below: where the heaviest snow will fall, how districts decide on closures, and the safety steps to take at home and on the road.
A strong storm system is organizing over the Gulf of Alaska and pushing heavy precipitation north into the Interior. Unlike the brief early-October flurries that dusted the region, this storm taps into a deep feed of moisture. It will stall just long enough to pile up snowfall totals that are extraordinary for this early in the season.

chunks.title: Alaska Winter Storm Oct 19–22, 2026: Closures & Safety | SnowDayPlanner
chunks.text:
Most of the Interior should expect widespread 12 to 18 inches . Higher terrain and favored upslope zones will see much more: 18 to 30 inches in the most exposed areas, and up to 36 inches in the Eastern Alaska Range above 2,500 feet. Snowfall rates could reach 1 to 2 inches per hour in the heaviest bands. At that pace, road conditions can go from manageable to dangerous in less than an hour.
Timing matters as much as totals. The heaviest snow arrives first, but the wind comes with it — and wind is what turns a heavy snowfall into a life-threatening blizzard.
# Where the heaviest snow is expected
The National Weather Service in Fairbanks has issued Winter Storm Warnings for a broad swath of the Interior. The hardest-hit areas include:
Fairbanks and the surrounding Interior: 12–18 inches of widespread snow, with locally higher amounts possible on the hills.
Richardson Highway corridor: dangerous conditions expected, with heavy snow and blowing snow reducing visibility to near zero at times.
Delta Junction: significant accumulations plus strong winds creating blizzard-like conditions.
Tanacross to Dot Lake: included in the warnings, with heavy snow and gusty winds.

chunks.title: Alaska Winter Storm Oct 19–22, 2026: Closures & Safety | SnowDayPlanner
chunks.text:
Eastern Alaska Range (above 2,500 feet): the bullseye — up to 36 inches of snow possible.
If you are in any of these zones, assume the warning applies to you. Warnings at this level are issued only when forecasters have high confidence in both the amounts and the impacts.
# Why the wind is the biggest danger
Snow totals grab the headlines, but wind is what makes this storm dangerous. Gusts of 60 to 65 mph are expected in exposed areas and along mountain passes. That is strong enough to snap power lines, topple trees onto roadways, and create whiteout conditions even when the snowfall has briefly eased.
Blowing and drifting snow will be the biggest threat on the Richardson Highway and other exposed routes. In a whiteout, you can lose all visual reference to the road in seconds. Drivers cannot see lane markings, guardrails, or even the vehicle ahead. This is why the NWS describes travel as potentially “very difficult to impossible.”
# How bad will travel be?
Do not travel unless you absolutely must. The NWS language — “very difficult to impossible” — is reserved for storms that defeat plows, tow trucks, and emergency responders alike. Expect:

chunks.title: Alaska Winter Storm Oct 19–22, 2026: Closures & Safety | SnowDayPlanner
chunks.text:
Major highways, including the Richardson Highway and the Alaska Highway, to become partially or fully impassable during the heaviest periods.
Flight delays and cancellations at Fairbanks International Airport and regional airfields.
Snowplows unable to keep up during the heaviest bands; secondary roads may not be cleared for a day or more.
Whiteout conditions arriving suddenly, even on road segments that seemed fine minutes earlier.
If you must drive, tell someone your route and expected arrival time. Carry a full emergency kit: blankets, food, water, a phone charger, a flashlight, and extra fuel. Be ready to turn back. A car that slides off the road in a whiteout is a survival situation — treat it that way before you start the engine.
# Will schools close? How to read the signs
For parents, this is the big question — and the short answer is that closures and delays are very likely in the warning zone. Districts across the Interior decide closures based on three things: road safety for buses, whether staff can get to school, and whether buildings can be kept heated and staffed. A 12- to 30-inch snowfall with 65 mph gusts and whiteouts checks every box.

chunks.title: Alaska Winter Storm Oct 19–22, 2026: Closures & Safety | SnowDayPlanner
chunks.text:
Districts typically announce decisions early in the morning — often between 5:00 and 6:30 a.m. — based on the overnight accumulation and the current state of the roads. Here is how to stay ahead of the announcement:
Check your district's official channels first. School websites, district social media accounts, and local radio stations carry the final, authoritative word. Our estimates are guidance; the district makes the call.
Run your ZIP through a closure predictor. Our free snow day predictor and school closing predictor turn live forecast data into a 0–95% closure probability score, so you can see the same math before the announcement drops.
Watch for the pattern. When a district delays once, it often delays or closes again the next day while roads are cleared — plan backup childcare for Wednesday and Thursday, not just Tuesday.
Expect remote-learning notices. Some districts pivot to remote instruction rather than a full closure. Know your child's login and have devices charged tonight.

chunks.title: Alaska Winter Storm Oct 19–22, 2026: Closures & Safety | SnowDayPlanner
chunks.text:
Rural and highway-dependent routes — exactly the corridors this storm is hitting hardest — are the first to be canceled and the last to resume. If your bus travels the Richardson Highway corridor, assume disruption through at least Wednesday.
# Driving safety checklist
If you cannot avoid driving during this storm, work through this checklist before you leave — and honestly, reconsider whether the trip is essential:
Check conditions before you go: visit the NWS Fairbanks forecast page and 511.alaska.gov for current road reports. If a warning was upgraded to a blizzard warning, stay home.
Slow down — radically: stopping distances on packed snow and ice can be 10 times longer than on dry pavement. Drive at half the posted speed or less in heavy snow.
Increase following distance: leave at least 8–10 seconds of gap between you and the vehicle ahead. If someone is tailgating you, let them pass.
No sudden moves: accelerate, brake, and steer gently. If you skid, ease off the gas and steer where you want to go — do not slam the brakes.

chunks.title: Alaska Winter Storm Oct 19–22, 2026: Closures & Safety | SnowDayPlanner
chunks.text:
Keep your lights on: daytime running lights are not enough in whiteout conditions. Turn on your headlights and, if visibility drops, your hazard lights — but never stop in a travel lane.
If you get stuck: stay with your vehicle. Tie a bright cloth to the antenna, run the engine 10–15 minutes per hour for heat (with the exhaust pipe cleared of snow), and crack a window to prevent carbon monoxide buildup.
Watch for black ice under the snow: temperatures hovering near freezing mean wet snow on top of ice — the slickest possible combination, especially on bridges and overpasses.
# Home and power-outage safety checklist
With 65 mph gusts forecast, power outages are a real possibility — and in Interior Alaska, losing heat in late October is an emergency, not an inconvenience:
Charge everything now: phones, power banks, laptops, and medical devices. An outage can arrive with the first big gust.
Prepare your heat backup: if you have a wood stove or generator, make sure it is fueled and ready. Never run a generator indoors or in a garage — carbon monoxide kills silently. Keep it at least 20 feet from the house.

chunks.title: Alaska Winter Storm Oct 19–22, 2026: Closures & Safety | SnowDayPlanner
chunks.text:
Protect your pipes: let faucets drip slightly, open cabinet doors under sinks on exterior walls, and know where your main water shutoff is.
Stock the essentials: three days of food that does not need cooking, a gallon of water per person per day, flashlights (not candles), batteries, and any prescription medications.
Keep fridge and freezer closed: an unopened fridge keeps food safe for about 4 hours; a full freezer for about 48. When in doubt, throw it out.
Check on neighbors: elderly residents and anyone with medical equipment that needs power should have a plan — or a place to stay.
Report outages, don't assume: call your utility; if lines are down in your area, assume they are energized and stay at least 30 feet away.
Warnings are currently in effect through Thursday, October 22 , and forecasters will refine snowfall totals as the storm's track firms up. After this system clears, the pattern stays active: early signals point to another snow window for the southern Rockies around October 23–24 (Colorado took 6–12+ inches from the October 13–15 system), which could set up the season's first big ski-resort dumps.

chunks.text:

# Frequently asked questions
# How much snow will Fairbanks get?
The NWS Fairbanks forecast calls for 12 to 18 inches across much of the Interior including Fairbanks, with 18 to 30 inches in favored higher-terrain zones and up to 36 inches in the Eastern Alaska Range above 2,500 feet.
# Will schools be closed tomorrow in the Fairbanks area?
Closures and delays are very likely given 12+ inches of snow, 65 mph gusts, and whiteout travel conditions. Districts usually announce by 5:00–6:30 a.m. — confirm with your district's official channels. You can also check our school closing predictor for a live probability score.
# Is it safe to drive the Richardson Highway during the storm?
No — the NWS warns travel may become “very difficult to impossible.” Heavy snow plus blowing snow will create whiteout conditions along the corridor. Delay travel until warnings are lifted.
# How long will the storm last?

chunks.title: Alaska Winter Storm Oct 19–22, 2026: Closures & Safety | SnowDayPlanner
chunks.text:
Winter Storm Warnings are in effect through Thursday, October 22. The heaviest snow falls earliest in the event, with winds and drifting continuing through the warning period.
# What should I do if I lose power during the storm?
Stay warm with layers and blankets, never run a generator indoors, keep the fridge closed, and check on vulnerable neighbors. Report downed lines to your utility and assume they are energized.

chunks.title: El Niño Winter 2026–27: Snow Forecast by State | SnowDayPlanner
chunks.text:
# El Niño Winter 2026–27: Snow Forecast by State
A strong El Niño is forecast for winter 2026–27, and for most of North America that means a stormy, snow-loaded season. The South and East should see an active storm track and above-normal snow chances. The Midwest sits in the path of frequent systems. The Pacific Northwest, by contrast, leans warmer and drier than normal. The practical result for families: more storms, and more mornings when schools have to decide whether to close.
Winter is already arriving early. October storms — from Alaska's 30-inch blizzard to Colorado's early-season dumps — are an early sign of the pattern ahead. Below: a plain-English explainer of how El Niño works, a region-by-region outlook for snow, and how to use our free snow day predictor to turn long-range hype into morning-of answers all season long.
# What is El Niño, and why does it matter this winter?
El Niño is a natural climate pattern defined by warmer-than-average water in the central and eastern tropical Pacific. That warm pool shifts the jet stream — the high-altitude river of air that steers storms across the United States — and with it, the track every winter storm follows.

chunks.title: El Niño Winter 2026–27: Snow Forecast by State | SnowDayPlanner
chunks.text:
In a typical El Niño winter, the southern branch of the jet stream (the subtropical jet) becomes unusually strong and active . That means more moisture streaming into the southern U.S., more Gulf of Mexico storm systems, and a storm track that favors the South and Southeast. Meanwhile, the Pacific Northwest and northern Rockies often turn warmer and drier. The Northeast becomes a battleground between Arctic air and Atlantic moisture — exactly the setup that produces big coastal snowstorms.
Strength is what makes this year different. Weak El Niños often have little influence; strong ones tend to produce the classic outcomes described here. Early indicators — including ocean temperatures already running well above normal — suggest 2026–27 could deliver one of the more typical strong El Niño winters in recent memory.
# The two big players in the models
Two features keep showing up in seasonal model runs, and together they explain most of the winter outlook:

chunks.title: El Niño Winter 2026–27: Snow Forecast by State | SnowDayPlanner
chunks.text:
A deep Gulf of Alaska low: models persistently place a deep area of low pressure in the Gulf of Alaska. This acts like a pump, sending Pacific storm energy into the West Coast and — critically — dragging Arctic air southward on its eastern side. When that cold air meets moisture from the subtropical jet, the result is big storm systems over the central and eastern U.S.
An active subtropical jet: the southern jet stream is forecast to be stronger than normal, carrying moisture from the Pacific across the southern tier of states and into the Gulf of Mexico. November is already showing an unusually wet signal, which matters — wet Novembers in El Niño years often foreshadow active storm tracks all winter.
The combination is classic: cold air available to the north, a steady stream of moisture to the south, and a storm track running right between them. That is the recipe for a busy winter.
# Regional outlook: state by state
# Northeast (New England, New York, Pennsylvania, New Jersey)

chunks.title: El Niño Winter 2026–27: Snow Forecast by State | SnowDayPlanner
chunks.text:
The Northeast is the winter's biggest wild card. El Niño does not guarantee a snowy Northeast — but it raises the odds of big coastal storms (nor'easters) when Arctic air does plunge south. With an active subtropical jet feeding moisture into the Atlantic, any cold-air outbreak can rapidly become a major snow event from Washington, D.C., to Boston. Expect near-normal seasonal totals but above-normal chances of one or two blockbuster storms — the kind that close schools across multiple states at once.
# Midwest (Illinois, Michigan, Ohio, Wisconsin, Minnesota)
The Midwest sits squarely in the storm track this winter. Frequent clipper systems and Colorado lows are likely, with above-normal snowfall for the Great Lakes snowbelts in particular. Lake-effect snow could be prolific early in the season before the lakes cool. For Michigan families: this has the makings of a top-tier snow-day winter — bookmark our Michigan snow day calculator . One caveat: periodic warm intrusions could mix rain into some events, especially south of I-80.
# Rockies (Colorado, Utah, Wyoming, Montana)

chunks.title: El Niño Winter 2026–27: Snow Forecast by State | SnowDayPlanner
chunks.text:
The southern Rockies look like a winner . The active subtropical jet points directly at Colorado and Utah, and October is already delivering: the October 13–15 system dropped 6 to 12+ inches, and another window around October 23–24 is on the models. Ski resorts from the San Juans to the Wasatch could see an early and deep base. The northern Rockies, closer to the warm Pacific Northwest influence, look closer to normal.
# The South (Texas, the Gulf Coast, the Southeast)
This is the classic El Niño zone — and the “ Winter Battleground ” ice-and-snow zone across the Mid-Atlantic and Southeast bears watching. The strong subtropical jet brings frequent Gulf moisture and storm systems; when even shallow cold air is in place, the result is ice storms and surprise snow events in places that rarely see them. Southern families should expect a wetter-than-normal winter with above-normal chances of at least one memorable ice or snow event . Ice is the real danger here — even a quarter-inch can close schools across entire metro areas.
# Pacific Northwest (Washington, Oregon)

chunks.title: El Niño Winter 2026–27: Snow Forecast by State | SnowDayPlanner
chunks.text:
The Northwest is the region most likely to be warmer and drier than normal — the classic El Niño outcome. That does not mean no snow; the Cascades will still get their storms. But the odds tilt toward fewer lowland snow events around Seattle and Portland. Ski areas at higher elevation should still do fine, while valley snow-day chances run below average.
Alaska is already living the active pattern — the October 19–22 Interior blizzard (up to 30 inches, 65 mph gusts) is exactly the kind of early-season storm the Gulf of Alaska low produces. Expect a stormy, warmer-than-normal winter for much of the state, with the Interior and Southcentral seeing frequent systems. Snow-day chances in Fairbanks and Anchorage run above normal, driven more by storm frequency than by extreme cold.
# What this means for snow days
A strong El Niño winter with an active storm track is, statistically, a high snow-day winter for the eastern two-thirds of the country. More storms mean more mornings where districts have to make the call — and more mornings where the forecast is genuinely uncertain until the last minute.

chunks.title: El Niño Winter 2026–27: Snow Forecast by State | SnowDayPlanner
chunks.text:
That is exactly what our tools are built for. The snow day predictor turns the next 24 hours of forecast data into a transparent 0–95% closure probability, and the school closing predictor is tuned specifically to district decision patterns. Long-range seasonal outlooks tell you what kind of winter to expect; our predictors tell you whether tomorrow is the day. Check tomorrow's score every evening once the storms start rolling — in an El Niño winter, you will use it a lot.
# Frequently asked questions
# Does El Niño mean a snowy winter for my state?
It depends where you live. El Niño favors a wet, stormy southern U.S., an active storm track through the Midwest and East, and a warmer, drier Pacific Northwest. The Northeast tends to see bigger individual storms rather than consistently cold, snowy weather. See the regional outlook above for your area.
# How accurate are winter seasonal forecasts?
Seasonal forecasts capture broad tendencies — wetter here, warmer there — but cannot predict individual storms months ahead. Treat them as a guide to the season's character, and rely on short-range tools like our snow day predictor for day-to-day decisions.

chunks.title: El Niño Winter 2026–27: Snow Forecast by State | SnowDayPlanner
chunks.text:
# When does the snow season usually start in the Rockies?
High-elevation Colorado resorts often see their first significant snow in October — and this year is no exception, with 6–12+ inches October 13–15 and another system possible October 23–24. Most ski areas aim to open by mid-to-late November.
# What is the “Winter Battleground” zone?
It is the Mid-Atlantic and Southeast corridor where cold Arctic air and warm Gulf moisture collide — producing the ice storms and surprise snow events that define El Niño winters in the South. Even small amounts of ice there cause widespread school closures.
# Will this be a record snow winter?
Records are possible in favored spots — especially the southern Rockies and snowbelts downwind of the Great Lakes — but “record” depends on individual storm luck as much as the pattern. What is highly likely: an active, memorable winter with plenty of snow-day mornings east of the Rockies.
